unit.title: Organize, prepare and present simple dishes

summary: This unit teaches you to organise your work in a villa or small hotel kitchen and to prepare, cook and present simple dishes safely: read a recipe, work out amounts and times, check and store ingredients, keep food safe, use knives and equipment safely, cook simple Jamaican and everyday dishes, and serve them hot or cold at the right time. You also learn to portion and plate food, clean as you go and report problems.

blocks.p: This unit is about being organised in the kitchen. A cook who plans, prepares and checks as she works serves good food on time and keeps guests safe. A cook who does not plan runs out of an ingredient, starts the stew too late and serves cold food. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. It is the base for the other kitchen units: basic methods of cookery, salads, sandwiches and cleaning the kitchen.

Villa guests may be on holiday from abroad or Jamaicans on a family weekend. Many have allergies or special diets, and many expect real Jamaican food, well cooked and neatly served. The work is as much about **planning, safety and care** as it is about cooking.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's kitchen, for example a Jamaican breakfast for four guests and a two-course lunch. Each member of the group must prepare and cook, and the assessor also watches your planning, hygiene, safety, plating and clean-down.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Photograph your practical stages: the plan, the preparation, the cooking, the plated food and the clean kitchen. Photograph hands, food and equipment, not people's faces, unless they agree and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Good cooks do most of their work before the stove is lit. Planning has three parts: knowing **what** to cook, **how much** to make and **when** to start each job.

A **recipe** is a written list of ingredients, amounts and method for one dish. A **standard recipe** is the one a kitchen always uses, so the dish tastes the same each time and the cost is known. Read the whole recipe before you start. Check that you have every ingredient and every piece of equipment, and that you understand each step. If a word is unfamiliar, ask your instructor or head cook.
**Mise en place** (say 'meez on plahs') is a French term for 'everything in its place'. Before you start to cook, you:

ul: wash your hands and put on a clean uniform, apron and hair cover;
weigh and measure the ingredients;
wash, peel and cut the vegetables, and trim and season the meat or fish;
get out the pots, pans, knives, boards, spoons and serving dishes you need;
put the ingredients in small bowls or trays in the order you will use them, with the raw meat kept apart in the fridge until needed.

blocks.p: When mise en place is done, cooking is quick and calm. You do not stop to hunt for a spoon while the onions burn.

blocks.h: Changing the amount a recipe makes

blocks.p: Recipes are written for a set number of portions. To cook for a different number, find the **scaling factor**:
**Scaling factor = portions you need ÷ portions in the recipe.** Multiply every amount by it.

head: Example
Working
Answer
rows: A recipe for 4 portions uses 600 g of pumpkin. You need 10 portions.
A recipe for 12 portions uses 3 cups of flour. You need 4 portions.
4 ÷ 12 = one third; then 3 cups × one third
1 cup
A recipe for 8 portions uses 2 litres of stock. You need 20 portions.
20 ÷ 8 = 2.5; then 2 litres × 2.5
5 litres

blocks.note: Scaling is not exact for everything. Salt, pepper, hot pepper, baking powder and spices should be added a little at a time and tasted, because a very large pot does not need exactly five times the seasoning of a small one. Cooking times and pot sizes also change: a very large pot of stew takes longer to heat through.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Working out the cost of a portion

blocks.p: Kitchens must know what a dish costs. **Cost per portion = total cost of the ingredients ÷ number of portions.** If the ingredients for a pot of soup cost JMD 4,800 and it makes 16 portions, one portion costs 4,800 ÷ 16 = JMD 300. This is why every portion must be the same size: if you give some guests more, the cost goes up and the profit goes down.

A **time plan** lists every job, how long it takes, and when it must start. You build it **backwards from the serving time**: the dish that takes longest is started first, and quick jobs are done last, so that all the food is hot and ready together.

flow: List every dish and job
Find how long each one takes, including resting and plating time
Start at the serving time and count backwards
Write the start time next to each job
Check that you are never doing more at once than you can manage
Pin the plan up where you can see it

head: Job
Time needed
Must start by
rows: Soak saltfish (overnight is best)
Several hours
The evening before
Brown stew chicken: marinate, brown, stew, rest
Marinate 1 hour or more; 15 min browning; 40 min stewing; 5 min rest
About 2 hours before serving if the marinade is made on the day
Rice and peas, once the peas are cooked
About 30 minutes, then 10 minutes to rest
About 45 minutes before serving
Steamed callaloo
10 to 15 minutes
About 20 minutes before serving
Dress the salad and warm the plates
A few minutes
Just before serving

blocks.note: A common mistake is forgetting resting time and plating time. If lunch is at 1:00 p.m., food should be ready to plate at about 12:50 p.m. Allow time to warm plates, wipe rims and garnish.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: In Jamaica, a power cut or a water lock-off can happen at any time. Know the villa's backup: a gas stove, a water tank and a torch. When you plan a meal for guests, ask how much cooking water the tank holds and fill pots and a clean drum before you start.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Planning the order and the stock

ul: Work out the total amount of each ingredient for the number of guests.
Check the store room, fridge and freezer. Write down only what is missing.
Order or buy in good time. Fresh fish, vegetables and bread may need ordering a day ahead.
Ask guests early about allergies, religious food rules and special diets such as vegetarian or vegan. Write them on the order.

blocks.p: Food poisoning is caused by bacteria, viruses and poisons that get into food. It can make guests very ill, and in a villa the guests are on holiday and far from their own doctor. Safe food handling protects the guest, the business and you. It rests on four ideas: **clean hands and clothes, keeping hot and cold food at the right temperature, keeping raw and cooked food apart, and cleaning properly**.

head: Habit
Why it matters
rows: Clean uniform and apron every day; change if soiled
Dirty clothes carry germs onto food.
Hair tied back and covered with a hat or hairnet
Stops hair falling into food, and stops you touching your hair.
Short, clean, unpolished nails; no false nails
Dirt hides under long nails; polish and false nails can chip into food.
No rings (except a plain band), watches or bracelets
Germs hide under them, and they can fall into food or catch in machines.
Cover cuts with a waterproof, coloured plaster and a glove
A cut is full of germs. A coloured plaster is easy to see if it falls into food.
Do not work if you have vomiting, diarrhoea, a fever or an infected sore; tell your supervisor
You can pass the illness to every guest. Staff who are ill stay off food work until they are well, as the Centre or employer's rules say.
Do not smoke, eat, chew gum or taste food with your fingers in the kitchen
Germs from your mouth and hands get onto the food.
Do not cough or sneeze over food; use a tissue and wash your hands
Droplets carry germs.

flow: Wet your hands with warm running water
Apply soap
Rub palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs and nails for at least 20 seconds
Rinse well
Dry with a clean paper towel
Turn off the tap with the paper towel

blocks.p: Wash your hands:

ul: before you start work and when you return to the kitchen;
before you touch ready-to-eat food;
after touching raw meat, fish, chicken, eggs or unwashed vegetables;
after using the toilet, touching bins, rubbish or cleaning cloths;
after touching your face, hair, nose or mouth, or blowing your nose;
after eating or drinking, and after handling money or a phone.

blocks.note: Use the hand-wash basin for hands only: never for washing food, pots or cleaning cloths. Hand sanitiser is useful after washing, but it does not replace washing, because it does not work well on visible dirt or grease.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Every food handler in Jamaica needs a **Food Handler's Permit**. It is issued through the local health department (the parish health department of the Ministry of Health and Wellness) and normally involves a health check and food safety training. Keep it where it can be seen or shown to an inspector, and renew it when it runs out.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Bacteria grow fastest between about **5 °C and 63 °C**. This is the **danger zone**. In warm food, some bacteria can double in number every 20 minutes or so. The way to control them is to keep food either **cold** or **hot**, and to keep the time in the danger zone as short as possible.

head: Rule
Typical figure
Notes
rows: Keep cold food, fridges and salads cold
5 °C or below
A fridge is checked and the temperature written in a log twice a day.
Keep frozen food frozen
Minus 18 °C or colder
Food that has thawed must not be refrozen.
Cook chicken, minced meat and reheated food right through
Core temperature about 74 °C
Measure the thickest part with a clean probe thermometer.
Keep hot food hot until served
63 °C or above
Use a bain-marie or hot cupboard, not a counter.
Cool leftovers quickly
A common guide: from 63 °C to 21 °C in 2 hours, then to 5 °C in 4 more hours
Use shallow trays; never put a very hot large pot straight into the fridge.

blocks.note: These figures are a common guide. The Centre's food safety plan and the business's own plan may set slightly different figures. Always follow the plan you work under, and your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Clean and sanitise the probe before and after each use.
Push the tip into the **thickest part** of the food, not touching bone or the pan.
Wait for the reading to settle. For chicken, a clear reading of about 74 °C, held for the time the plan says, means it is cooked.
Check the thermometer regularly, as the maker says, by testing it in iced water (about 0 °C) and boiling water (about 100 °C at sea level).

blocks.p: **Cross-contamination** is the passing of bacteria from raw food, dirty hands, cloths or equipment onto food that will not be cooked again. Salad, fruit, bread and cooked meat are the foods most at risk.

head: Where it can happen
How to prevent it
rows: In the fridge
Store raw meat, fish and chicken in covered trays on the bottom shelf, below cooked and ready-to-eat food, so that juices cannot drip down.
On boards and knives

Use separate, colour-coded boards and knives. A common code: red for raw meat, blue for raw fish, yellow for cooked meat, green for salad and fruit, brown for vegetables, white for dairy and bread. Follow the Centre's code.
On hands
Wash hands after raw food and before ready-to-eat food. Use tongs or clean gloves for ready-to-eat food.
On cloths and surfaces
Use separate cloths. Never wipe a raw-chicken board with the cloth you use on the salad board. Clean and sanitise surfaces after raw food.
During delivery and storage
Keep raw and cooked food in separate covered containers. Keep vegetables with soil on them away from ready-to-eat food.

blocks.p: Do not wash raw chicken under the tap. It splashes germs around the sink and does not make the chicken safe. Cooking does that.

An **allergen** is a substance in food that can cause a harmful reaction in some people. A reaction can be a rash or swollen lips, but it can also be a severe reaction (anaphylaxis) that stops breathing, and can kill. The most common food allergens are peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, fish, shellfish (shrimp, lobster, crab), wheat and gluten, soya and sesame.

ul: Ask guests about allergies when the order is taken, and write them on the order. Tell the head cook.
Read the label of **every** ingredient, including stock cubes, sauces, seasoning, margarine, bread and crackers. Allergens hide in these.
Use clean boards, knives, pots and oil for an allergy meal. Cook it first, and keep it covered and labelled.
Treat every allergy seriously, even if the guest says it is 'only a mild one'.
Never guess. If you are not sure whether a dish contains an allergen, say so and ask the chef.

blocks.note: Coconut milk is not dairy milk, but a guest with a nut or milk allergy may still ask about it. Give the guest the full ingredient list, let her decide, and ask the head cook.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: When a delivery arrives, check it **before** you sign. Look at the order sheet, count the items, check the quality and the temperature, and check dates. Chilled and frozen food must go into the fridge or freezer straight away, before you unpack anything else.

head: Food
Accept it if
Reject it if
rows: Chilled meat, chicken, milk and eggs (chilled)
At 5 °C or below; fresh smell; clean packs; within the date
Warm to the touch or above 5 °C; sour smell; sticky, slimy or discoloured; damaged packs; out of date
Frozen food
Frozen hard; no ice crystals inside the pack; at minus 18 °C or colder
Soft or partly thawed; lots of ice crystals or a pool of liquid in the pack, which suggests it has thawed and refrozen
Fresh fish
Clear, bulging eyes; bright red gills; firm, shiny flesh; fresh sea smell; packed in ice
Sunken, cloudy eyes; dull or brown gills; soft flesh; strong fishy or ammonia smell
Fruit and vegetables
Firm, fresh colour, no mould or rot
Bruised, soft, mouldy, wilted or slimy; insects
Eggs
Clean shells with no cracks
Cracked, dirty or leaking
Tins and cans
Undamaged, labelled, in date
Swollen or bulging, deeply dented, rusty or leaking tins. Do not open or taste them.
Dry goods (flour, rice, cornmeal)
Dry, sealed, no insects or smell
Torn bags, damp, lumpy, insects or droppings

blocks.p: If you reject something, tell the supervisor, write it on the delivery sheet and send it back with the driver. Never accept a poor item 'just this once'.

head: Where
What goes there
Rules
rows: Fridge (5 °C or below)
Meat, fish, dairy, eggs, salads, cooked leftovers, open tins decanted into containers
Covered and labelled. Raw food on the bottom shelf, cooked above. Do not overfill, so cold air can move. Check the temperature in the morning and write it in the log.
Freezer (minus 18 °C or colder)
Frozen meat, fish, ice
Label with date. Never refreeze thawed food.
Dry store
Rice, flour, cornmeal, sugar, tins, oil
Cool, dry, clean and off the floor, on shelves. Keep covered and sealed against pests.
Vegetable rack
Onions, potatoes, yam, green bananas, pumpkin
Cool, dark, ventilated, off the floor. Keep ripe fruit away from green bananas.
Chemicals
Cleaners and disinfectants
A separate cupboard, away from food, in labelled containers.

blocks.p: Put new stock **behind** the old stock and use the oldest first. Check the 'use by' and 'best before' dates every day. A **use-by** date is about safety: do not use food after it. A **best-before** date is about quality: the food may still be safe, but it will not be at its best.
Every container of prepared food in the fridge needs a label with **what it is and the date and time it was made**, and the use-by date. Many kitchens also add the cook's initials and any allergens.

ul: Best: thaw in the fridge, in a covered tray on the bottom shelf, for as long as it takes (a whole chicken can need a day or more).
Never thaw on the counter or in warm water: the outside gets warm while the middle is still frozen.
If the plan allows, a sealed pack can be thawed under cold running water, but only for as short a time as possible and the food cooked straight away.
Do not refreeze food that has fully thawed unless it has been cooked first.

head: Ingredient
What to know
rows: Ackee
Use only **fully ripe ackee from pods that have opened by themselves on the tree**
Remove the black seeds and the pink-red membrane; wash the yellow flesh; boil gently and throw the water away
Unripe or forced-open ackee contains a poison (hypoglycin) that can cause serious illness. Canned ackee from an approved source is safe to heat and use
Saltfish (salted cod and similar)
Soak or boil in fresh water, once or twice, to take out most of the salt. Taste a piece before you use it. Remove skin and bones and flake.
Callaloo
A leafy green. Wash well to remove soil and grit; cut off tough stems.
Escallion
Jamaican name for spring onion (scallion).
Thyme and pimento
Thyme: the herb, used in most savoury dishes. Pimento: allspice berries, used in jerk, stews and escoveitch.
Scotch bonnet pepper
Very hot. Wear gloves, do not touch your eyes, and wash hands and board after. Add whole to a pot of rice or soup for flavour without the heat, taking care not to burst it.
Red kidney beans

Dried beans must be soaked, then **boiled hard for at least 10 minutes** and simmered until soft, because raw or under-cooked beans contain a poison that causes vomiting. Throw away the soaking water.
Green bananas and yam
Peel, wash and boil in salted water. Green banana sap stains hands and clothes.
Coconut milk
Fresh, canned or powdered, it gives rice and peas its flavour. Not dairy milk.

head: Knife
Use
rows: Cook's (chef's) knife
General cutting and chopping of vegetables, meat and herbs.
Paring knife
Small jobs: peeling, trimming, and cutting small vegetables and fruit.
Bread (serrated) knife
Slicing loaves and soft items such as tomatoes.
Boning knife
Taking meat off the bone.
Palette knife
Spreading and lifting. It is not for cutting.

ul: A **sharp** knife is safer than a blunt one. It needs less force, so it is less likely to slip.
Cut on a steady board. Put a damp cloth under it so it does not slide.
Curl the fingers of your guiding hand, so the knuckles guide the blade. Cut away from your body.
Carry a knife **point down, close to your side**, and say 'knife' or 'behind' as you pass people.
Never try to catch a falling knife. Step back and let it fall. Pick it up by the handle.
Wash knives one at a time and never leave them in a sink of soapy water where you cannot see them. Dry and store them in a block or on a magnetic strip.
Never use a knife to open tins, cut string or stir hot food.
Choose a pot the right size, with a thick base for stews and rice, so food does not burn.
Turn pan handles inwards, away from the edge of the stove and out of the way of people passing.
Use **dry** oven cloths, because wet cloth carries heat and can scald you.
Lift lids away from your face so that the steam goes away from you.
Do not overfill pots. Never carry a full pot of hot liquid through a busy kitchen; ask for help and shout 'hot'.
Light gas stoves as the maker says. If you smell gas, switch off, open windows, leave the area and tell your supervisor; do not use switches or flames.
Dry the food before it goes into hot oil. Water makes the oil spit and splash.
Never fill a pot of oil more than about half full. Heat gently and never leave it alone.
Lay food into the oil **away from you**.
Let oil cool completely before you move or strain it.

blocks.note: If a pan of oil catches fire: turn off the heat, and slide a lid, a baking tray or a fire blanket over the pan. **Never use water**: it makes the fire explode outwards. Do not move the pan. Raise the alarm and use the correct extinguisher if the fire spreads. Know where the fire blanket and extinguisher are before you start.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Do not use a machine you have not been trained to use.
Check guards are in place and the plug and cable are undamaged before use. If a guard is broken, do not use the machine: report it and use another one.
Switch off and unplug the machine before you clean it, change a blade or clear a jam.
Never put your hand into a blender jug or the mixer bowl while it is running. Use a spoon or spatula only when it has stopped.
When blending hot soup, fill the jug no more than half, keep the lid on and hold it down with a cloth. Hot liquids expand and can blow the lid off.

blocks.h: Preventing slips, trips, burns and strains

ul: Wipe up spills at once and put out a wet-floor sign.
Wear closed, non-slip shoes.
Keep walkways clear of boxes, bags and cables.
Lift with bent knees and a straight back. Ask for help with heavy pots and sacks.
Report any injury, however small, and write it in the accident book. Know where the first aid kit is.

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V, 50 Hz. Check that every appliance is made for it; a blender made for 220 V will not work, and an adapter can be a fire risk. Keep electrical equipment away from sinks and wet floors.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: This section covers the simple cooking skills and dishes that the unit asks for. The methods are explained again in the unit on basic methods of cookery; here you learn how to use them to cook a simple meal.

head: Method
What it is
Good for
rows: Boiling
Cooking in water at about 100 °C (at sea level), with big bubbles.
Green bananas, yam, eggs, saltfish, pasta.
Simmering
Cooking in liquid just below boiling, with small bubbles.
Soups, stews, rice and peas, dumplings.
Poaching
Cooking gently in liquid that is not boiling.
Eggs, fish.
Steaming
Cooking in the steam above boiling water, with the food not in the water.
Callaloo, fish, vegetables.
Stewing
Long, slow cooking in a little liquid in a covered pot.
Tough cuts such as oxtail and goat; brown stew chicken.
Frying
Cooking in hot fat or oil: shallow or deep.
Fish, dumplings, festival, plantain.
Baking and roasting
Cooking with dry heat in an oven.
Bread, cakes, whole chicken, vegetables.
Grilling
Cooking quickly with strong heat from above or below.
Chops, fish, sausages.

flow: Soak the saltfish (overnight is best), or boil it in fresh water once or twice; taste to check that most of the salt has gone
Skin, bone and flake the fish
Prepare the ackee: if it is fresh, use only ripe ackee from naturally opened pods; remove the black seeds and pink-red membrane; wash, boil gently and drain; if it is canned, drain it
Heat a little oil. Sweat the chopped onion, escallion, sweet pepper and thyme until soft
Add the flaked saltfish and tomato and cook for a few minutes
Fold in the ackee very gently so it does not break up
Season with black pepper and a little scotch bonnet; taste. Add salt only if needed
Serve hot, with fried dumplings, boiled green banana or festival

ul: **Fried dumplings:** mix flour, a pinch of salt and water to a firm dough; knead lightly, rest for 15 to 20 minutes, shape into small rounds or fingers, and shallow-fry in oil over medium heat, turning, until golden and cooked through.

**Festival:** a slightly sweet fried dumpling. Mix flour, cornmeal (roughly one part cornmeal to three or four parts flour), sugar, salt, baking powder and a little water or milk into a stiff dough. Shape into finger lengths and fry in hot oil until golden brown. Drain on kitchen paper.
Oil that is too cool makes greasy dumplings; oil that is too hot browns the outside while the inside stays raw. Test with a small piece of dough: it should sizzle and rise steadily.

blocks.p: Cut off the ends, slit the skin lengthways, boil in salted water for about 15 to 20 minutes until a knife goes in easily, then peel. Yam is peeled first, cut into pieces and boiled until tender. Do not leave either in the water after they are cooked, or they become soggy.

Wash the callaloo well, cut off the tough stems and chop the leaves. Sweat chopped onion, tomato, escallion and thyme in a little oil, add the callaloo, cover and steam in its own moisture for about 10 to 15 minutes, until just tender. Callaloo cooked for too long turns grey and loses its flavour, colour and vitamins.

flow: Soak dried red kidney beans overnight; throw away the water
Boil the beans hard for at least 10 minutes, then simmer until soft
Add coconut milk, water, escallion, thyme, pimento berries, a whole scotch bonnet pepper and salt, and bring to the boil
Wash the rice and stir it in
Cover tightly and cook on low heat until the liquid is absorbed, about 20 to 25 minutes
Remove the pepper without bursting it; fluff with a fork and let it rest for 5 to 10 minutes

blocks.p: A common guide is about twice as much liquid as rice by volume. The exact amount depends on the rice and the recipe. Do not keep lifting the lid or stirring: it makes the rice mushy.

flow: Cut the chicken into pieces; season with salt, black pepper, garlic, onion, escallion, thyme and a little browning; marinate in the fridge
Heat oil in a heavy pot and brown the chicken pieces on all sides, in batches, so the pot does not cool
Add sliced onion, sweet pepper, tomato and a little water or stock
Cover and simmer gently, stirring now and then, until tender and the gravy has thickened (about 30 to 40 minutes)
Check the core temperature of the thickest piece is about 74 °C
Taste and adjust the seasoning; rest for a few minutes before serving

blocks.p: Browning the chicken first gives colour and flavour. Overcrowding the pot makes the chicken boil in its own juices and turn grey.

Cut the Jamaican pumpkin into pieces, discarding the skin and seeds. Sweat chopped onion, garlic, escallion and thyme in a little oil, add the pumpkin, stock or water and pimento berries, and simmer until the pumpkin is soft. Many Jamaican soups also include carrot, yellow yam and 'spinners' (small finger-shaped dumplings). For a smooth soup, blend a little at a time, then reheat to piping hot, and taste. Serve in warmed bowls.

A **roux** is flour cooked in an equal amount of fat (butter or oil). It thickens sauces and soups. Melt the fat, stir in the flour and cook it for a minute or two without browning to take away the raw flour taste. Add warm liquid **a little at a time**, stirring or whisking, so that no lumps form. Simmer for about 10 minutes, and taste.

Wash lettuce, tomato, cucumber and carrot in cold water, drain and dry the leaves well, tear or cut into bite-size pieces, and chill. Dress just before serving, because the dressing makes the leaves soft and wet. A simple dressing is oil, lime juice or vinegar, salt and pepper.

ul: **Taste** with a clean spoon each time. Put the spoon in the sink after each taste; never put a used spoon back into the pot.
**Look**: colour (bright vegetables, golden fried food), consistency (not too thick or thin), no burnt bits.
**Smell and feel**: cooked vegetables are tender; fish flakes; rice grains are separate.
**Temperature**: use a probe thermometer for chicken, minced meat and reheated food, and to check hot-holding.
Season in stages and taste again. You can add salt but you cannot take it out.

blocks.p: A **portion** is the amount of one dish served to one person. Use the **same measure each time**: a ladle for soup and stew, a scoop or cup for rice, a weighed amount of meat or fish, a counted number of dumplings. Equal portions are fair to guests, keep the cost right and make the stock last for the right number of covers.

head: Item
Typical way to measure
rows: Soup
A ladle of the same size; fill to the same line in the bowl.
Rice
A cup, scoop or small mould.
Chicken or fish
Weigh before cooking, or count pieces.
Dumplings and festival
Count: for example two or three each.
Salad
A scoop or handful, or a set number of slices.

head: Point
What to do
rows: The plate
Clean, with no chips or cracks, and the right size so the food is not crowded or lost. Warmed for hot food (warm to the hands, not too hot to carry) and chilled for cold food.
Colour
Mix colours: green callaloo, orange carrot, yellow plantain, red tomato. A plate that is all brown or all pale looks dull.
Shape and height
Pile food slightly in the centre; arrange items in a neat group, not spread flat.
The main item first
Put the main item (the chicken, fish or ackee) first, then the starch and then the vegetables, with the sauce beside or under it.
The rim
Wipe any drips with a clean paper towel before the plate goes out.
Garnish
A small edible item that adds colour and flavour: a sprig of thyme, a slice of tomato, a little chopped escallion. It must go with the dish. Do not use inedible garnish.
Temperature
Hot food is served hot (63 °C or above) and cold food cold (5 °C or below).
Speed
Serve at once. Food on the pass that waits goes cold or gets warm.

blocks.note: Never put a garnish on a plate that you would not want the guest to eat. Check also that nothing on the plate came from a different guest's plate that was returned.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Hot food held for service must stay at 63 °C or above; use a bain-marie or hot cupboard, and cover it.
Cold food stays in the fridge or on ice until just before service.
Clean hands, tongs or serving spoons only; never your fingers.
Label dishes on a buffet with the name and any allergens.
Food that has stood out longer than the plan allows must be thrown away.

blocks.p: Clean spills and used tools while you work, so the kitchen never becomes a mess. Scrape plates and boards, wash used knives straight away, wipe the bench, and put rubbish in the bin. A clean kitchen is safer and quicker to work in.

blocks.h: Cleaning a board, bench or tool

flow: Scrape off food and waste into the bin
Wash with hot water and detergent
Rinse with clean water
Sanitise with a food-safe sanitiser, left for the time on the label
Leave to air-dry on a rack, or dry with a clean disposable cloth

blocks.p: **Air-drying** is better than a tea towel, because damp cloths carry germs.

blocks.note: Never mix bleach with other cleaning products. Bleach and an acid cleaner or an ammonia cleaner can give off a poisonous gas. Read the label and follow the dilution. Wear gloves and eye protection when the label says so. Store chemicals away from food, in labelled containers.
blocks.label: Safety

ol: Divide hot food into **shallow** containers so it cools quickly.
Cool it quickly, for example in iced water or a clean sink; stir to help.
When it has stopped steaming, cover, label with the name, date and time, and put it in the fridge.
Use within the time the plan allows (often 2 to 3 days).
Reheat until piping hot all through (about 74 °C), once only. Throw away any leftovers after reheating.

blocks.note: Cooked rice needs special care. Rice can carry spores of a bacterium (Bacillus cereus) that survive cooking. If rice is left warm, the spores grow and make a poison that reheating does not destroy. Cool rice within about an hour, refrigerate, and reheat only once.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Use lidded bins, lined with bags, and empty them often.
Keep food waste away from clean food and preparation areas. Wash your hands after touching a bin.
Take bin bags to the outside waste area, which is kept clean and covered, so that flies, rats and dogs do not get to it.
Let used cooking oil cool, store it in a labelled container and have it collected as the Centre or villa arranges. Never pour it down the sink.

blocks.p: Tell your supervisor straight away about:

ul: a fridge or freezer at the wrong temperature;
broken or damaged equipment, such as a loose plug or missing guard;
signs of pests (droppings, chewed packets, cockroaches);
an injury or a near miss;
a food allergy or complaint from a guest;
stock that is low, damaged or out of date;
a power cut or water lock-off.

blocks.p: Write it in the log or report book with the date, time and what you did. Then put 'out of order' signs on faulty equipment.

ul: I can explain mise en place and list what I do before I cook.
I can scale a recipe up or down and work out the cost of one portion.
I can write a time plan by counting back from the serving time.
I can describe good personal hygiene and say when to wash my hands.
I can name the danger zone and the temperatures for cold storage, hot holding and cooked chicken.
I can explain cross-contamination and how colour-coded boards, fridge storage and clean hands prevent it.
I can take an allergy order and say what I must do to keep the guest safe.
I can check a delivery and decide what to accept or reject.
I can store, label and rotate food, and thaw frozen food safely.
I can make fresh ackee and saltfish safely, including making the ackee safe.
I can choose the right knife and use, carry and clean it safely.
I can fry safely, and say what to do if oil catches fire.
I can cook simple dishes: boiled food, callaloo, rice and peas, dumplings, brown stew chicken and a simple soup.
I can taste, check quality and portion food evenly.
I can plate food neatly on warm or chilled plates with a suitable garnish.
I can clean as I go, cool and store leftovers and handle waste correctly.
I can report faults, hazards and temperature problems.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I cook the chicken to about 74 °C in the thickest part, so that any bacteria are killed.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Having ingredients and equipment prepared and ready before you cook.
A written list of ingredients, amounts and method for one dish.
The recipe a kitchen always uses, so a dish is the same every time.
The number you multiply a recipe by: portions needed divided by portions in the recipe.
A list of jobs with start times, worked out backwards from the serving time.
The amount of one dish served to one person.
The range from about 5 °C to 63 °C, where bacteria grow fastest.
The temperature in the thickest, coolest part of food.
A thermometer pushed into food to measure its core temperature.
Bacteria passing from raw food, hands or equipment onto food that will not be cooked again.
Chopping boards of different colours, each used for one kind of food.
A substance in food that can cause a harmful reaction in some people.
First in, first out: use the older stock first.
The date after which food is not safe to eat.
The date until which food is at its best quality.
The permit every food handler in Jamaica needs, issued through the health department.
Salted, dried fish that must be soaked or boiled before use.
To cook in liquid just below boiling, with small bubbles.
Cooking in the steam above boiling water.
Long, slow cooking in a little liquid in a covered pot.
Flour cooked in an equal amount of fat; used to thicken sauces.
A small edible item added to a dish for colour and flavour.
A product that reduces germs on clean surfaces to a safe level.
To let washed items dry in the air on a rack, instead of using a cloth.

c1.title: Birthday lunch for ten in Negril
c1.text: Chef Marcia Grant is asked to cook a birthday lunch for 10 guests at a villa in Negril, to be served at 1:00 p.m. Her standard recipe for brown stew chicken is written for 4 portions and uses 1.2 kg of chicken and 600 ml of water. The chicken needs 15 minutes to brown and 45 minutes to stew, and she wants it to rest for 5 minutes before plating. The chicken has to be seasoned and marinated first.

c2.title: A delivery at a villa in Port Antonio
c2.text: At 9:30 a.m. a supplier's van delivers to a villa kitchen in Port Antonio. The driver is in a hurry. Cook Delroy checks the goods. The snapper fillets are firm, shiny and packed in ice. The cartons of milk read 9 °C on his probe. A tin of ackee has a swollen, bulging lid. The frozen chicken is soft at the edges, with a pool of liquid and many ice crystals in the bag.

c3.title: Fresh ackee from a neighbour in Gordon Town
c3.text: A neighbour brings a basket of ackee to the villa where Andre is the cook. Some pods are fully open by themselves, showing yellow flesh. Others are only half open, and a few are still closed and red. The neighbour says the closed ones will open on the kitchen counter by tomorrow. Andre is cooking ackee and saltfish for 8 guests tomorrow morning. The saltfish is in a dry packet.

c4.title: A guest with a milk allergy in Montego Bay
c4.text: Mr. Ian Chen tells the cook at a Montego Bay villa that his 7-year-old daughter is allergic to milk. The planned menu is pumpkin soup finished with cream, callaloo cooked in butter, rice and peas, and cornmeal porridge made with condensed milk. The cook is not sure whether the stock cubes or the margarine on the shelf contain milk.

c5.title: Sunday lunch leftovers in Mandeville
c5.text: After a Sunday lunch for 12 at a villa in Mandeville, Shanice leaves a large pot of rice and peas and a pot of stew on the stove for three hours while guests relax. She then puts both pots, still warm, straight into the fridge with the lids on. Next morning the fridge thermometer reads 9 °C, and the temperature log shows it was at 4 °C the evening before.

c6.title: Plating lunch for twelve in Treasure Beach
c6.text: Kevon is plating steamed fish, rice and peas, boiled green banana and steamed callaloo for 12 guests at a villa in Treasure Beach. The fish portions he has cut vary between 160 g and 220 g. The callaloo has gone a dull grey-green. The plates are white with nothing on them but pale rice, pale banana and brown fish.

questions.q: How much chicken does Chef Marcia need for the 10 guests?
o: 3.0 kg
2.4 kg
3.6 kg
4.8 kg
questions.why: The scaling factor is 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5, and 1.2 kg × 2.5 = 3 kg, which is 300 g for each guest. Check the working twice, because a wrong figure means short portions or wasted food.

questions.q: Working back from 1:00 p.m., when must she start browning the chicken?
o: 12:00 noon
questions.why: Add the times: 15 minutes browning + 45 minutes stewing + 5 minutes resting = 65 minutes. 65 minutes before 1:00 p.m. is 11:55 a.m. Cooking begins even earlier if the plan includes plating and warming plates.

questions.q: Which job should Marcia put first in her time plan?
o: Slice the cucumber and tomato for the salad
Season the chicken and leave it to marinate
Warm the dinner plates in the oven for service
Make the salad dressing and pour it into jugs
questions.why: Marinating needs the most time, so it is started first. Quick jobs such as the salad and warming plates are done last, so the food is fresh and hot together.

questions.q: All the ingredients for the 10 portions cost JMD 6,200 in total. What is the cost of one portion?
o: JMD 620
JMD 62
questions.why: Cost per portion is the total cost divided by the number of portions: 6,200 ÷ 10 = JMD 620. Equal portions keep this cost the same for every guest.

questions.q: Which delivered item may Delroy accept without a problem?
o: The ackee tin, because the contents are sealed from the air
The cartons of milk, because they are still sealed
The frozen chicken, because it will be cooked well anyway
The snapper fillets that are firm, shiny and packed in ice
questions.why: Firm, shiny fish packed in ice is fresh and cold. The other items are warm, damaged or have partly thawed, and cooking does not make that food safe again.

questions.q: What should Delroy do with the tin of ackee with the swollen lid?
o: Open it carefully and smell the contents before deciding
Refuse it and record it, and not open it or taste it
Put it at the back of the shelf and use it last
Boil the whole tin, unopened, to make it safe
questions.why: A swollen tin can mean bacteria are growing and making gas inside. It is sent back unopened and noted on the delivery sheet; it must never be tasted.

questions.q: The milk reads 9 °C. What is the best action?
o: Accept it and chill it quickly, because it is still sealed
Accept it, but use it first so that it is finished today
Accept it and add it to cooked dishes where it will be heated
Reject it, because chilled food must arrive at 5 °C or below
questions.why: Chilled food above 5 °C is in the danger zone and may already be unsafe. Check it with a probe, reject it and write the reading on the delivery sheet. Using it up soon does not fix it.

questions.q: Which pods may Andre use?
o: The half-open pods too, because the yellow flesh is already visible
Only pods that opened fully on their own on the tree
The closed pods, once he has opened them by hand tomorrow
Any pod, once the black seeds have been taken out
questions.why: Only ackee from pods that have opened naturally on the tree, which means the fruit is ripe, is safe. Unripe or forced-open ackee contains hypoglycin, a poison; removing seeds does not make it safe.

questions.q: After removing the seeds and membrane from the good ackee, what does he do next?
o: Wash it, boil it gently and throw the water away
Fry it straight away in oil with the onions and thyme
Boil it, then use the water as stock in the dish
Steam it over the saltfish water to save time
questions.why: Boiling and draining makes ackee ready to cook, and the water is thrown away because it may carry traces of the poison. Never use it as stock.

questions.q: Andre boils the saltfish once and the flaked fish is still very salty. What should he do?
o: Add extra ackee to balance the saltiness
Boil it again in fresh water, and taste again
Add a spoon of sugar to the pan to hide the salt
Skip the salt and add more scotch bonnet pepper
questions.why: Saltfish is boiled or soaked in fresh water, once or twice, until most of the salt has gone. Tasting a piece tells you when it is ready; ackee, sugar or pepper do not remove salt.

questions.q: What should the cook do first about the girl's allergy?
o: Leave out the cream and carry on with the other dishes as planned
Ask the guest to bring the girl's own food to the table
Tell the head cook, and check the label of every ingredient
Use a separate spoon and serve the dishes as planned
questions.why: The head cook must know, and every ingredient, including stock cubes and margarine, must be checked, because milk hides in many foods. Taking out one obvious item is not enough.

questions.q: How should the callaloo be changed for the girl?
o: Cook it in the same pan, but with less butter
Cook it in butter, then rinse the butter off the leaves
Cook it as planned and serve her a smaller portion
Cook it in oil that has no milk in it, in a clean pan
questions.why: The butter must be left out and replaced with oil in a clean pan. Even a small amount of milk can cause a reaction in an allergic person, so reducing or rinsing is not safe.

questions.q: Mr. Chen says the reaction is only a rash. How should the cook take this?
o: As a serious allergy, with full care as for any allergy
As a mild allergy, so a trace of milk is acceptable
As a dislike, so the girl can have a little milk if she wants
As a problem for the parents only, not the kitchen
questions.why: A reaction that starts as a rash can become severe next time. All allergies are handled with full care, and the kitchen must never decide that a risk is small.

questions.q: What was wrong with the way Shanice handled the two pots?
o: They sat 3 hours in the danger zone, then warmed the fridge
She covered both pots with lids, which kept the heat in the food
She cooled them in the fridge, which spoils the flavour
She waited for the guests to finish before putting food away
questions.why: Food left standing for hours spends too long between 5 °C and 63 °C, where bacteria multiply. Big warm pots also heat the fridge. Food should be divided into shallow containers and cooled quickly.

questions.q: Why is the cooked rice a particular risk?
o: Rice soaks up bacteria from the pot water and keeps them inside each grain
Rice goes bad faster in the fridge than any other cooked food does
Spores survive cooking, then make a poison that reheating cannot destroy
Rice cannot be reheated safely because it dries out and goes hard
questions.why: The spores of a bacterium called Bacillus cereus survive cooking. If the rice is left warm they grow and make a poison that stays harmful after reheating, so rice must be cooled fast and kept cold.

questions.q: The log shows 4 °C last night and 9 °C this morning. What should be done with the stew in that fridge?
o: Reheat it to 74 °C, which makes the stew safe to serve whatever happened
Serve it today, but make sure no guest takes a second helping
Check how long it was above 5 °C; discard it if over the plan's time
Move it into the freezer, where the bacteria will stop growing
questions.why: How long the food stayed warm decides whether it is safe, and the plan sets the time allowed. Reheating cannot destroy every poison, and freezing does not kill bacteria. Report the fault and move the other food to a cold fridge.

questions.q: What most likely made the callaloo go dull and grey-green?
o: It was steamed instead of boiled
It was washed too many times
It was cooked for too long
It was left in too little water
questions.why: Callaloo should be steamed for a short time (about 10 to 15 minutes) until just tender. Overcooking turns it grey and takes away the flavour, colour and vitamins.

questions.q: Which change would most improve how the plates look?
o: Fill the plate with a bigger scoop of rice and banana
Cover the fish with a thick sauce to hide its colour
Put a large sprig of parsley on the rim of every plate served
Add the callaloo and tomato slices for colour and height
questions.why: A plate of pale food looks dull. A mix of colours, with the food slightly raised in the centre and a garnish that suits the dish, looks fresh and inviting, as long as the garnish is edible.

questions.q: Kevon's fish portions vary between 160 g and 220 g. What is the best way to fix this?
o: Cut by eye, as an experienced cook can judge it
Weigh each portion before cooking, to the same amount
Serve the larger portions to the adults only
Give each guest the same number of pieces whatever the size
questions.why: Weighing gives equal portions, which is fair to every guest and keeps the cost per portion right. Cutting by eye or counting pieces gives different amounts.

questions.q: What must be done to dried red kidney beans before the rice and peas is cooked with them?
o: Soak them overnight and add them to the rice with the water they soaked in
Add them dry to the rice, since the long cooking time will soften them
Soak them, boil them hard for at least 10 minutes, then simmer until soft
Rinse them and leave them in a warm place until they begin to sprout
questions.why: Raw or under-cooked red kidney beans contain a poison that causes vomiting. Boiling hard for at least 10 minutes destroys it, and the soaking water is thrown away.
